title: Data Interpretation
weightage: 5–10 questions (a full DI set in Tier 1 & Tier 2)
intro: Data Interpretation is arithmetic with a chart attached: tables, bar graphs, pie charts and line graphs. There is no new theory — every question is a percentage, ratio, average or total in disguise. The marks go to whoever reads the chart accurately and computes fast, so the skills from the percentage, ratio and average chapters pay off directly. The discipline that wins: read exactly what is asked, pull only the numbers you need, and approximate when the options are far apart.

items.name: Pie chart
items.formula: value = (sector angle / 360) x total, or percent x total

topics.name: Tables
topics.details: A table lists exact values in rows and columns — the cleanest DI form because no reading-off-a-scale error is possible. Scan the row/column headers first so you know where each number lives, then answer with totals, averages, ratios or percentages. Watch the units stated in the caption.

solved.problem: A shop sold (in units) Mon 20, Tue 25, Wed 15, Thu 30, Fri 10. Total for the week?
From the same data, the average daily sale?
What percent of the week's sales happened on Thursday?
Ratio of Monday to Wednesday sales?

topics.name: Bar Graphs
topics.details: Each bar's height is a value; read it against the axis scale. Questions ask for totals across bars, the difference between two bars, percentage change from one year to the next, or which bar is largest/smallest. With grouped/stacked bars, identify the segment before computing.

solved.problem: Production (in tonnes) over 2019-2022: 40, 50, 60, 50. Total?
Percentage increase from 2019 (40) to 2021 (60)?
Average production over the four years?
By what percent did 2022 (50) fall from 2021 (60)?

unsolved.problem: Difference between largest and smallest of 30,45,25?

topics.name: Pie Charts
topics.details: A pie chart splits a whole (the total) into sectors. A sector's value = (its angle / 360) x total, or simply percent x total when given in percents. To convert a percent to an angle, multiply by 3.6 (since 100% = 360 degrees). Always note the stated grand total before computing any slice.

solved.problem: A budget of 7200 is split: Food 25%. Food amount?
A sector is 90 degrees of a total of 4000. Its value?
Convert 30% to a sector angle.
If Rent is 120 degrees of a 9000 budget, the rent?

topics.name: Line Graphs
topics.details: A line graph tracks a value over time; the slope shows the trend. Questions ask for the value at a point, the change or percent change between two points, the steepest rise/fall, or the average over the period. Read each point against the axis, and for percent change always divide by the earlier value.

solved.problem: Visitors (in thousands): Jan 10, Feb 14, Mar 12, Apr 18. Total?
Percent rise from Jan (10) to Apr (18)?
Average monthly visitors?
Between which consecutive months was the rise largest?
solved.solution: Jan->Feb +4, Feb->Mar -2, Mar->Apr +6; largest rise Mar->Apr.

topics.name: Mixed & Caselet DI
topics.details: Caselet DI gives the data as a short paragraph (no chart) and may combine two data sets (a table plus a pie, or two bars to compare). Extract the numbers into your own mini-table first, then it is ordinary arithmetic. Multi-step questions (find a total, then its percentage, then a ratio) reward writing intermediate values down rather than holding them in your head.

solved.problem: A class has 120 students: 60% boys. Number of girls?
Of 48 girls, 25% play a sport. How many?
Two shops sell 200 and 300 units; what percent of the combined total is shop A?
A sells 200 at profit 20%, B sells 300 at profit 10%. Whose absolute terms are larger if unit cost is equal at 100? (profit per unit)
solved.solution: A profit/unit 20, total 4000; B profit/unit 10, total 3000; A is larger (4000 vs 3000).

unsolved.problem: Shops 150 and 350; A is what percent of total?
Combined total of 240 and 360, then 25% of it?

shortcuts: DI is just percentage/ratio/average — no new theory.
Percent to pie angle: multiply by 3.6; angle to percent: divide by 3.6.
Percent change always divides by the EARLIER value.
Approximate when options are far apart; compute exactly only when they are close.
Write intermediate totals down in multi-step caselets.
mistakes: Dividing by the new value instead of the old in percent change.
Misreading the axis scale or the units in the caption.
Using the wrong grand total for a pie slice.
Computing every value when the question asks for only one.
pyq: SSC always includes at least one full DI set (table/bar/pie/line). Tier 2 adds caselet and two-source DI. Speed and accurate reading decide the marks, not new formulas.
summary: Treat every chart as arithmetic: read the values accurately, then apply percentage, ratio or average. Convert pie percents to angles with x 3.6, divide by the old value for percent change, and approximate when the options allow.
